problem: Robots executing natural language navigation instructions may produce motions that do not match what human users expect, and it is unclear which variations of robot behavior humans judge as appropriate.
motivation: Human-robot teaming improves when robot actions meet human expectations. The study asks which action variations humans judge as matching expectations for instructions drawn from a human-robot dialogue corpus.
key_idea: Run a human-judgment study in which 21 volunteers rate variations of a virtual robot's behavior while it executes eight navigation instructions from a human-robot dialogue corpus.
insight: Per the abstract, movement more accurately meets human expectation when the robot navigates with awareness of its environment and demonstrates a sense of self-safety. Only the abstract was available, so no ablation details can be given.
method: Human-judge study: 21 volunteers evaluate a virtual robot's behavior.
Stimuli: eight navigation instructions taken from a corpus of human-robot dialogue.
Behavior variations: different robot action variants per instruction, compared by judges against their expectations (details not given in the abstract).

setting.backbone: none (human evaluation of a virtual robot)

results: Initial findings suggest that human judges' expectations are better met when the robot navigates with environment awareness and shows self-safety. No quantitative results are given in the abstract.
limitations: Small study (21 volunteers, eight instructions), with findings described as initial.
Evaluated on a virtual robot only, not a real robot.
